---
title: Time series forecasting
description: "Predict future values from observed history, series context, and covariates known at each forecast cutoff."
engine: markdown
---

Suppose a retailer has hourly sales for each store and product, plus a promotion
schedule published in advance. It wants forecasts for the next few hours to
support replenishment decisions. One observation will describe a store-product
series at a cutoff, its completed sales history, and the future hours to score.

The model below combines numeric targets and repeated contexts for that
dataset. Compare it with simpler forecasts on the same replenishment
decisions to assess whether those contexts help.

## Describe history and the requested horizon

Let `at` mean the end of an hourly bucket. At a May 28 cutoff of 10:00, all
history buckets have completed. The application supplies three requested
future buckets, ending at 11:00, 12:00, and 13:00. The promotion flags were
already known at 10:00. A historical training observation receives the
future `units` labels after those buckets complete:

```yaml
series_id: store-17_milk-1l
history:
  - at: "2026-05-28T08:00:00Z"
    age_hours: 2
    units: 8
  - at: "2026-05-28T09:00:00Z"
    age_hours: 1
    units: 11
  - at: "2026-05-28T10:00:00Z"
    age_hours: 0
    units: 10
horizon:
  - at: "2026-05-28T11:00:00Z"
    lead_hours: 1
    promotion: false
    units: 12
  - at: "2026-05-28T12:00:00Z"
    lead_hours: 2
    promotion: true
    units: 16
  - at: "2026-05-28T13:00:00Z"
    lead_hours: 3
    promotion: true
    units: 14
```

The entire record is one observation. `history.units` is observed input;
`horizon.units` is a future target. Their separate schema addresses allow the
same field name to have those different roles. Retain the series identifier
and cutoff when associating forecasts with source records.

## Build a model for those records

The declared numeric, categorical, and calendar fields generate encoders for
this dataset. The two branches specify observed history and future requests;
the masked numeric field puts a prediction objective at every requested
horizon record. Together they define the forecasting model's architecture
and learning task:

```python
import relflow as rf

model = rf.Model.xs(
    series_id=rf.Category,
    history=rf.Branch(
        length=168,
        overflow="tail",
        at=rf.DateParts(dateparts=["day_of_month", "day_of_week", "hour_of_day"]),
        age_hours=rf.Number,
        units=rf.Number,
    ),
    horizon=rf.Branch(
        length=24,
        overflow="error",
        at=rf.DateParts(dateparts=["day_of_month", "day_of_week", "hour_of_day"]),
        lead_hours=rf.Number,
        promotion=rf.Boolean,
        units=rf.Number(mask=True),
    ),
)
```

Order the history oldest to newest; it keeps the latest 168 completed hourly
observations. The horizon accepts
up to 24 requested hours; the three slots above request three forecasts.
`length=24` sets a limit. The application still constructs each future record
and timestamp.

`DateParts` supplies calendar cycles, while `age_hours` and `lead_hours` express
elapsed time relative to the cutoff. Your application calculates those
durations. The model can learn relationships between recent demand, calendar
position, and planned promotions across the training observations.

At prediction, keep the observed `history.units`. Omit `units` only from the
`horizon` records, leaving their timestamps, lead times, and known promotion
flags. The returned `predictions.horizon` contains one numeric result per
requested future record, in its retained order. It returns three results for
this request, with no padding to 24.

Use application-prepared Parquet files with this structure and follow
[Train and save](../learn/train-and-save.qmd) with forecasting-specific file
paths. The [prediction contract](../reference/prediction-output.qmd) describes
the numeric result envelope.

## Prepare a forecast as it would have been known

Choose whether a series is regular hourly data or an irregular event history.
For hourly demand, assemble the hourly grid before making observations. A
verified hour with no sales can be zero; an unavailable hour is missing data.
RelFlow's branch ordering and calendar fields do not infer which situation
occurred or fill missing hours.

Here `units` measures recorded sales. A stockout can suppress those sales, so
the example's target is observed sales under the retailer's availability
conditions. Estimating unmet demand needs additional availability information
and a corresponding target definition. Preserve stock and availability facts
as they were known at each cutoff when they enter a forecast.

Keep only completed, available history buckets. Use the promotion schedule
version known at the cutoff. A weather input for a future hour would need the
weather forecast issued by that cutoff, rather than the weather later
observed. Every `horizon.units` label remains masked, including when several
future targets share context.

Train on many historical cutoffs and series. Field normalization is learned
across that field's training observations; declaring `series_id` does not
create a separate automatic normalizer for each series. Decide how source
units and large differences in series scale should enter the comparison.

## Evaluate at the requested lead times

Compare the same series, cutoffs, and requested hours with these baselines:

| Baseline | Forecast |
| --- | --- |
| Last observed value | Repeat the latest completed hourly value. |
| Seasonal naive | Reuse the corresponding hour from a prior day or week, with the lag chosen on validation data. |
| Existing forecasting model | Use the same observed history and genuinely known future inputs. |

These simple benchmarks are described in
[Forecasting: Principles and Practice](https://otexts.com/fpp3/toolbox.html).
Measure MAE or RMSE separately by lead time and across the series that matter
to replenishment. Check whether a pooled metric hides weak performance on
low-volume series. Test across later cutoffs, ensuring training labels and
their reporting delays complete before the evaluation period. Compare the
same chosen horizons throughout.

The model above produces point forecasts. Prediction intervals require a
separate uncertainty method and coverage evaluation; a `Quantile` field's
percentile encoding is not a forecast interval. If demand decisions require
nonnegative outputs or accounting constraints, define that output policy and
evaluate the resulting forecasts. See [Evaluation](../learn/evaluation.qmd).

## Adapt the series and its context

For **load or sensor forecasting**, replace `units` with the measured quantity
and add device or site attributes, maintenance events, and known schedules
when available. Irregular measurements need explicit elapsed durations.

For **market bars**, a record can keep opening, high, low, closing prices, and
volume together. To predict the next trading day's close, supply only
completed bars and define the next trading session explicitly. Compare with
the last observed close on the same sessions and forecast horizon.

For **multiple related series**, decide which other measurements were available
at each cutoff and how their histories belong in the observation. Nested
branches provide structure; the application supplies the alignment and
relationships. [Relational prediction](relational-prediction.qmd) explains
that preparation, while [Customer outcomes](customer-outcomes.qmd) covers
future totals over a fixed outcome window.
